newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia shrugs off delay in U.S. F-16 sale.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia shrugs off delay in U.S. F-16 sale.

text.p: Indonesia said on Friday it was not bothered by a delay in its purchase of F-16 fighters from the United States because of Jakarta's human rights record, adding it could look elsewhere for its aircraft needs.
"From the beginning, the possibility of purchasing F-16s has not been a priority for Indonesia," State Secretary Murdiono told reporters.
"If they want to cancel the deal, we do not have any objections. If we need planes, we can buy from other countries."

Asked about a U.S. State Department spokesman's comments that the purchase was complicated by an Indonesian government crackdown on political dissent, Murdiono said: "Many other countries also have problems on human rights."
Spokesman Glyn Davies said in Washington on Thursday the U.S. government had postponed notifying Congress of the sale until the legislature reconvenes next year.
Formal Congressional notification is necessary prior to the sale and gives the legislature 30 days in which it can, if it wishes, pass a resolution of disapproval.

The United States has been hoping to sell to Indonesia nine F-16s out of a batch of 28 originally sold to Pakistan but whose delivery was blocked by a Congressional amendment prompted by Islamabad's nuclear policy. The proceeds would be used to reimburse Pakistan.
Davies said the decision to delay the sale had been taken in response to concerns in Congress over violence in Jakarta in July. He said those concerns were shared by the administration.
But, he added: "We are still convinced the sale is in the U.S. national interest and should proceed."

Riots erupted in Jakarta on July 27 after police raided the headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party and evicted supporters of ousted party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri, daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno.
At least five people died and scores of buildings and vehicles were set on fire during the violence, the worst in the city for more than 20 years.
The government later took more than 200 people into custody and charged several with subversion, a crime punishable by death.
